title: Use maps to access and communicate information concerning routes, location and direction

lessons.title: What a map shows: key, scale and direction
lessons.html:
Why maps are useful on a farm

A map is a drawing of a place seen from above. Farm maps show the houses, camps, roads, dams, fences, gates and boundaries. Maps help you find your way, explain to a driver where to deliver feed, show the fire break route or tell emergency services how to reach the farm.

The key (legend)

Maps use small symbols and colours instead of drawing every detail. The key or legend is a box that tells you what each symbol means. For example:

  • Blue = water, such as a dam, river or borehole.
  • Black squares = buildings, like poultry houses or the farm office.
  • A dashed line = a gravel or farm road.
  • A line with small crosses = a fence.

Always read the key first before you use a map.

Directions: the compass

The four main directions are North (N), East (E), South (S) and West (W). On most maps North is at the top. A small arrow marked N shows which way North is. Between them are North-East (NE), South-East (SE), South-West (SW) and North-West (NW).

A way to remember: in South Africa the sun rises in the east and sets in the west. In the middle of the day the sun is in the northern part of the sky.

Scale

A map is much smaller than the real place. The scale tells you how much smaller. A scale bar might show that 1 cm on the map = 100 m on the ground. If two poultry houses are 3 cm apart on the map, they are 3 × 100 = 300 m apart in real life.

A scale can also be written as a ratio, like 1 : 10 000. This means 1 cm on the map is 10 000 cm (100 m) on the ground.

lessons.title: Finding locations and planning routes
lessons.html:
Finding a place on a map

Many maps have a grid of squares. The columns have letters (A, B, C...) and the rows have numbers (1, 2, 3...). A grid reference like C4 tells you to go across to column C and then up or down to row 4. The place you want is in that square. Town maps, road maps and many farm maps use this system.

Today many people also use a phone with GPS, which gives a location as numbers (co-ordinates) or a pin on a map app. You can send this pin to a delivery driver or an ambulance. It is still important to know landmarks, because phone signal can be weak in rural areas.

Describing a route

A route is the way you travel from one place to another. When you give directions, be clear and use landmarks:

  1. Start: "From the main gate on the tar road..."
  2. Direction and distance: "...drive north on the gravel road for about 2 km..."
  3. Landmarks: "...past the big dam on your left..."
  4. Turns: "...turn right (east) at the second gate..."
  5. End: "...the broiler houses are the four long buildings ahead."

Choosing the best route

The shortest route is not always the best. Think about:

  • Road condition – a gravel road may be impassable after rain.
  • Biosecurity – feed and egg trucks should not drive past dead-bird or manure areas, and visitors' vehicles may need to stop at the wash bay first.
  • Safety – avoid routes past heavy machinery or through camps with bulls.
  • Low bridges or narrow gates for big trucks.

Working out distance

Measure the route on the map with a piece of string along the road, then lay the string on the scale bar. If the string measures 8 cm and 1 cm = 250 m, the route is 8 × 250 = 2 000 m, which is 2 km.

lessons.title: Drawing simple maps and plans
lessons.html:
Making your own map

Sometimes you need to draw a quick map: to show a new worker where the feed store is, to mark where a fence is broken, or to show the route for a fire drill. A simple, clear sketch map is very helpful.

Steps to draw a sketch map

  1. Draw a North arrow in a corner.
  2. Start with the main things: the road, the main buildings and the dam.
  3. Try to keep sizes and distances roughly in proportion. Things far apart should look far apart.
  4. Add smaller details: gates, taps, the dip tank, the dead-bird pit, the fire extinguishers.
  5. Use simple symbols and make a key.
  6. Add a title and the date.

Emergency and evacuation maps

Every workplace should have an emergency plan. A map near the door of each house can show:

  • Where the exits are.
  • The safe assembly point where everyone meets after leaving a building.
  • Where fire extinguishers and the first aid box are kept.

Learn the map for your work area. In a fire or emergency, walk quickly to the assembly point by the route shown. Never go back into a burning building for belongings.

Explaining where the farm is

If you must phone for an ambulance or the fire service, give clear information: the farm name, the nearest town, the road number and distance from a well-known landmark, such as "12 km past the Engen garage on the R40, turn left at the green farm gate." If you can, send a GPS pin and ask someone to wait at the gate to guide them in.

Key points

  • Read the map key first to understand the symbols.
  • North is usually at the top; know N, E, S and W.
  • Use the scale to change map distance into real distance.
  • Grid references and GPS pins help you find exact places.
  • Give routes with directions, distances and landmarks.
  • Know the emergency map and assembly point for your work area.

quiz.question: What part of a map tells you what the symbols mean?
On a map 1 cm = 100 m. Two houses are 3 cm apart on the map. How far apart are they really?
In which direction does the sun rise?
What does the grid reference C4 tell you?
